Mr. Shanti Ranjan Karmaker, Advocate  ------- For the Petitioner. 
Mr. Md. Wahidullah, Advocate  ------- For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Narayan Chandra Banerjce alias Bandapadhya ------- Defendant Petitioner
Vs.
Md. Salek Ali Shaik  ------- Plaintiff Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
Habibur Rahman Khan, J: On an application filed under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the defendant No. 2 Petitioner, this Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment & decree dated 20th March, 1982 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka reversing the decision of the Munsif 4th Court, Munshiganj passed on 31.12.79 in Money Suit No.1 of 1979 should not be set aside. 

 2. The suit being money suit No.1 of 1979 was filed by the opposite party Md. Sudek Ali Shaik @ Sadek Ali as plaintiff for the recovery of the consideration money amounting to Tk. 7,500.00 from the defendants. The plaintiffs case, in short, was that the plaintiff purchased the suit land measuring 63 decimals from the defendants for a consideration of Tk. 10,000.00 (taka ten thousand) only on 9.9.78. Subsequently, on scrutiny, it transpired that the defendants were owner to the extent of 1/4 th share only of the suit land. Accordingly, it was found that the plaintiffs kabala stands valid only to the extent of 1/4th share and no title passed to the plaintiff to the extent of remaining 3/4th share of the purchased land in question. So the plaintiff is entitled to get back Tk. 7,500.00 (Taka seven thousand and five hundred only) from the defendants. The suit was filed as the defendant did not pay back the money on demand made by the plaintiff. Only defendant No. 2 contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that they got the entire suit land by way of gift from their father Dinesh Chandra Bandapadhya who became the exclusive owner in possession of the same and, accordingly, by the purchase from the defendants valid title passed to the plaintiff over the entire suit land. While owning and possessing the suit land the defendants sold the same to the plaintiff and the plaintiff is in ownership and possession of the entire 63 decimals of land. Moreover, the plaintiff was fully aware about the title of his vendors, the defendants from before the purchase. The point for determination in the suit was whether the defendants sold the land without having 16 annas right, title and interest in the same and, if not, whether the plaintiff is entitled to get back from the defendants an amount of Tk. 7,500 being the 3/4 share of the consideration money out of the total consideration money paid by the plaintiff for the land. In the case plaintiff has examined himself as PW 1 and the defendant was examined as DW 1. The learned trial Court after examination of the witnesses and hearing arguments by his judgment and decree dated 31.12.79 dismissed the suit on contest against the defendant No. 2 and ex parte against the rest without cost. In the trial stage it was pleaded that the suit was hit by section 35 of the Specific Relief Act and the learned trial Court found that in the instant case sale and purchase of the suit land was concluded on plaintiff's payment of the consideration money and the defendants executing and registering the kabala and at this stage there remains nothing to be revoked or annuled by way of rescission. The learned trial Court also found that the plaintiff has failed to prove the fraud alleged to have been practised against the plaintiff. It was also found that the plaintiff purchased the suit land being fully aware about the title of the defendants in the same and that the plaintiff has also been in undisturbed possession of the suit land. 

 3. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the trial Court the plaintiff preferred appeal before the District Judge and the said appeal having been heard by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka was allowed and the suit was accordingly decreed. The appellate Court below did not reverse the finding of the trial Court to the effect that there has been no fraud and, therefore, the finding of the learned trial Court to the extent that section 35 of the Specific Relief Act is not applicable in the instant case, was found to have been affirmed. The learned appellate Court also affirmed the finding of the learned trial Court that the plaintiff has still been in possession of the entire suit land since purchase and has been enjoying the usufruct thereof. The appellate Court, however, decreed the suit with the finding that the defendants had title only to the extent of 1/4th share of the suit land and with regard to remaining 1/4th share of the suit land the vendors themselves having acquired no title, could not confer any valid title to the plaintiff. 

 4. Mr. SR Karmaker, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioner, after placing the judgment of both the courts, submits that the Court of appeal below approached the case from a wrong angle of vision and made out a third case himself and set aside the judgment and decree of the learned trial Court without reversing all the points raised, discussed and decided by the learned trial Court and hence the judgment and decree of the appellate Court below cannot be sustained. The learned Advocate further submits that it was nobody's case that 3/4th share of the demised property was vested property but the court of appeal below committed error of law and misdirected itself in assuming jurisdiction not vested in him in presupposing that the property is vested property and the defendants having no salable interest therein was liable to pay the compensation for damage in respect of the same. It is argued by Mr. SR Karmaker that the defendant's predecessor Dinesh Chandra Bandopadhya obtained 1/4th share by inheritance and 3/4th share by way of purchase from his three brothers vide kabala dated 8.10.71 (a copy of which was produced) and the defendants after obtaining right, title and interest in respect of the entire suit land from their father being in ownership & possession sold the same to the plaintiff. The learned advocate also argued that the plaintiff having been a borga cultivator under the father of the defendants and, thereafter, under the defendants was well aware about whatever title they had in the suit land before and at the time of purchase and, therefore, fraud could not be attributed to the vendors. 

 5. By referring to the case of Dalsukharam Saheba Vs. Mulchand Ashram reported in AIR 1928 (Bom) 427 (Rele. page 429). Mr. Karmaker submits that if the plaintiff with ordinary care could have discovered that there was defect.of title, then he cannot plead that there was failure on the part of the defendant to comply with the obligation laid down in s. 55(1)(a) Transfer of Property Act I find substance in the above submissions of the learned Advocate of the petitioner and I hold that the plaintiff is not entitled to say that there has been fraud on the part of the defendant in regard to the sale of the suit property to the plaintiff. 

 6. Mr. Md. Wahidullah, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party, by way of supporting the judgment and decree of the appellate Court below, submits that the defendant's father Dinesh Chandra Bandopadhya was no doubt owner to the extent of 1/4th share of the suit land but the rest 3/4th share belonged to his other three brothers and they being non-residents of the country their portion has become vested property and the defendant having sold the said land on fraudulent misrepresentation of fact the plaintiff has not acquired any title in respect of the same and for that matter the learned court of appeal below has rightly decreed the suit for the recovery of the 1/4th of the consideration money. In support of his contention Mr. Wahidullah cited the case of Injad Ali and others Vs. Mohini Chandra Adhikari reported in CWN Vol XXVII page 1025 and the case of Allahdino Bacha Vs. Udhumal Amardenomal reported in AIR 1942(Sind) page 82; The case reported in the XXVll CWN 1025 is different and distinguishable from the present one as the suit under reference was a suit also for the recovery of possession the plaintiff being not in possession of the suit land but in the instant suit the question of possession is not involved as the plaintiff after obtaining possession from the vendor has remained in possession without being disturbed by anybody. In the other cited case reported in 1942 AIR 82 the following observation has been made: 

 "Where the sale deed in favour of the plaintiff by the defendant was not a nullity which the plaintiff could ignore and the defendant had title to at least part of the property and the plaintiff obtained possession of at least part of the property, the only case which the plaintiff could advance is that the sale deed is voidable because of material defect in his vendor's title not disclosed by the vendor, such non-disclosure amounting to fraud under section 55, Transfer of Property Act. Plaintiffs remedy in such circumstance is a suit for rescission of the sale deed, and for return of the price paid under s.38, Specific Relief Act. It is not open for him to ask for return of the price before conveyance is rescinded". 

 7. The fact of the present case discloses that the plaintiff purchased the property with open eyes having opportunity to know the title of the defendant and that the plaintiff having obtained delivery of possession has still been in possession in respect of the whole of the property. That being the position the principle laid down in the above referred case does not help rather it goes against the plaintiff as the plaintiff is not entitled to ask for the return of the portion of the consideration money before the conveyance is rescinded in a duly constituted suit. 

 8. In the instant suit the suit land originally belonged to four brothers, viz. Dinesh, Jitendra, Bamkin and Sushen. Thereafter Dinesh became the owner in respect of 1/4th of the suit land by inheritance and the remaining 3/4 by way of purchasing the share of his three other brothers. While in ownership and possession of the suit land, Dinesh gifted the land to his three sons who are the defendants in the suit and the deed of gift was accordingly executed on 28.2.78 and registered on 4.3.78 in favour of the defendants. The gift deed contains a recital to the effect that Dinesh acquired property by way of inheritance from his father and also by way of purchase from his brothers. Furthermore, the present plaintiff being a borgader under Dinesh Bandopadhya and thereafter under the defendants was quite aware about whatever title defendants had in the suit land and, therefore, the question of defendants playing fraud does not arise. The next point raised by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite party is that the other three brothers of Dinesh having left the country their 3/4 share in the property has become vested and non-resident property and the defendant having acquired no title therein could not confer any title on the plaintiff by the sale in question. The plaintiff examining himself as PW 1 deposed that he saw the father of the defendants possessing the entire suit land. He said that he has been possessing the suit land and nobody ever questioned his possession. Thus it is found from the admission of the plaintiff that since purchase the plaintiff has all along been in possession of the suit land without any interference from any quarter. The plaintiff has failed to produce any scrap of paper from the vested property authority at any stage of the suit appeal and revision in support of the contention that 1/4 portion of the suit land has become vested property. The apprehension that the land will be taken by the vested property authority appears to be so vague and remote that such apprehension cannot give rise to any cause of action for the plaintiff to get any relief, particularly when the plaintiff has been owning and possessing the property without being disturbed or challenged by the vested property authority or anybody. I do not find any element of fraud being practiced on the plaintiff by the defendant in the transaction. The suit seems to be a misconceived one and the plaintiff is not entitled to any relief in the same and the suit was, therefore, rightly dismissed by the trial Court. The learned court of appeal below committed error of law in setting aside the judgment of the trial Court without adverting to all the points raised and decided by the learned trial Court making out a third case and hence the impugned judgment cannot be sustained in law.
